item.title: Parent Burnout and Special Needs Parenting
item.description:
Burnout

Parent Burnout and Special Needs Parenting

When caring for a child with special needs leaves little room for you.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Parenting a child with special needs can create an overwhelming mental and emotional load.
  • Burned-out parents often function in survival mode.
  • Burnout does not mean you are a bad parent.

Parenting is the hardest job I’ve ever had. I say that often to myself and to parents with whom I work. Parenting a child with ADHD, anxiety, autism, learning differences, or other special needs can add another layer of emotional and physical demands. Appointments, therapies, school meetings, evaluations, medications, homework, behavioral challenges, and constant communication with professionals can leave parents feeling like you’re always on and needing to keep track of the next detail or appointment. This can be a perpetual cycle with some moments of respite, but the demand is strong. This often leaves parents feeling overwhelmed, overextended, tired, and just plain old burned-out.

1. The Mental Load Is Real

The invisible and visible mental load is very real. Parents are remembering the big things like therapy schedules, advocating at school, and friendships, while also thinking about and anticipating your child’s potential triggers and how to challenge your child so he or she can continue to make progress. This constant sense of responsibility and anticipating what’s next leads to emotional exhaustion, irritability, difficulty sleeping, and eventually burnout.

There is also the emotional weight of constantly worrying about your child's future. Parents may find themselves wondering about what’s next and anticipating future obstacles within and outside of their child. When you are constantly anticipating the next challenge or trying to prevent the next crisis, it can become difficult to simply enjoy whatever the current moment may be, and instead sit in a place where you are surveying the past, and thinking about tomorrow, next month, and next year.

2. Your Relationship Can Get Lost in the Process

When so much attention is focused on a child's needs, the parent relationship often falls down to the last “to-do” item on the list. Daily interactions can become focused on the “business” of raising children and running a household. That leaves little time to connect with each other, maintain intimacy, and have time alone, without the children. Oftentimes, parents function in survival mode and stay there for long periods of time. This becomes a natural place for the marital or parental relationship to sit, but that doesn’t mean it needs to stay there.

Over time, couples may begin to feel more like co-workers managing a household than partners in a relationship. One parent may feel they are carrying more of the mental load, while the other may feel unsure of how to help. Resentment can build, even when both parents love their child and each other very much. Making space for the relationship is not selfish. A strong partnership provides emotional support for both parents and creates a sense of balance and alliance.

3. Burnout Does Not Mean You Are a Bad Parent

Many parents feel guilty when they admit they are exhausted. They may believe that because their child needs them, they should always have more patience, more energy, and more to give. But burnout is not a reflection of how much you love your child. In fact, it often develops because you have been giving so much for so long. Recognizing that you are overwhelmed is not selfish, but rather an important first step in giving yourself continued energy and resources to care for your child.

It is also important to remember that being a good parent does not mean being available every minute of every day. Your child can have needs that are important without those needs always having to be met by you. Learning to ask for help, set boundaries, and tolerate your child being upset with you or upset in general can actually build resilience for your child.

Strategies for Reducing Parent Burnout

Ask for Help and Delegate: Start by looking for ways to share the load rather than simply adding more self-care to your already-full schedule. Self-care can end up feeling like one more thing to schedule, carve out time for, and do. Ask your partner or family members or try to hire help.

Schedule a Small Break For You and Your Relationship: I'm not talking about scheduling a whole day. Schedule a small period of time, such as 30 minutes, to do something where you are walking away from responsibilities and engaging in something mindless. You can sit in silence, read, journal, or whatever calms your nervous system on a regular basis.

You can also do the same for time with your significant other. That is, schedule date nights or a night away. Take a walk together, even if it is in silence.

Set Boundaries: Although the to-do list can seem endless and the timeframes always seem urgent, set boundaries around work, school communication, and caregiving when possible. Have a start and end time for your job, for your care for the house, for sending and responding to emails, etc. It’s OK to stop and it’s OK to not get it all done. Prioritize and put what didn’t get done today on your list for the next day.

Parenting a child with special needs requires incredible energy, patience, and love. Your needs also matter as parents. Taking care of yourself is not selfish and it’s not a luxury, but rather a necessity. If you are coming in with a drained battery, your clarity, strength, and ability to problem-solve may be limited. Charge your battery so that you can take care of your child(ren).

item.title: 3 Reasons Why Looking Foolish Can Be Good for Your Brain
item.description:
Happiness

3 Reasons Why Looking Foolish Can Be Good for Your Brain

The surprising benefits of looking silly.

Posted September 10, 2026

Key points
  • Looking foolish is uncomfortable but survivable.
  • Play is good for adult mental health.
  • Being bad at new things helps your brain grow.

Public speaking is often listed among our greatest fears. As Jerry Seinfeld once joked, at a funeral, the average person would rather be in the casket than delivering the eulogy.

I have spent a truly impressive amount of my life trying to avoid looking foolish. Most people would agree.

There’s a spectrum when it comes to avoiding public humiliation. Being laughed at is generally considered to be an unpleasant experience. But there’s even a word for an extreme fear of it. Gelotophobia is a personality trait characterized by a disproportionate fear of being laughed at by other people (Torres-Marín et al., 2017).

Unfortunately, learning almost anything requires a period of being bad at it. If we want creativity, innovation, and play in our lives, learning to tolerate the discomfort of looking foolish is an important part of our adult development.

And looking foolish may actually be good for your mental health. Here are three reasons why.

1. It teaches your brain that embarrassment is survivable.

Your brain is built to care what other people think. Humans are social creatures, and belonging has always mattered for survival.

Research on social-evaluative threat shows that situations that threaten our social standing can trigger measurable psychological and physiological stress responses, including shame, anxiety, changes in heart rate, and increased cortisol (Bosch et al., 2009).

In other words, looking ridiculous can feel like a much bigger threat than it is.

Every time you do something awkward and survive it, your brain gets new information: I looked foolish and people saw me, but nothing terrible happened.

Avoiding embarrassment can make your world smaller, but when you can increase your window of tolerance for feeling foolish, your world and opportunities within it expand.

2. Being bad at something gives your brain something new to do.

Neuroplasticity means your brain has the capacity to change. The adage “You can't teach an old dog new tricks" is inaccurate according to research. No matter where you are in the lifespan, if you have a brain, there is still possibility to change. But in order to make changes in your life (and in your brain), you’ll need to expose your brain to new stimuli and disrupt its predictive and pattern-seeking functions.

Learning new skills is an instant “auto-pilot deactivate” button. When you learn a new skill, your brain has to stay present and adapt in real time. Research on skill acquisition has found both functional and structural changes in the brain as people practice and learn new things (Dayan & Cohen, 2011).

But in order to train your brain, you’ll need to become willing to be bad at new things.

3. Looking foolish gives you more access to play.

It’s easy to assume play is the domain of children. But research on adult play suggests that play can contribute to subjective and psychological well-being (Colston, 2023).

The benefits of play are well documented; play can help your brain problem-solve, and laughter itself has even been associated with reductions in cortisol (Kramer & Leitao, 2023). But play is inaccessible to a brain stuck on hypervigilance and perfectionism.

So if you want to train your brain and give yourself access to a lot more options, try running a low-stakes experiment. Intentionally trip over something in public. Maybe accidentally drop something in the grocery store. Then pay attention to what happens in the aftermath. If your experiment is low-stakes enough, the result will disconfirm your brain's belief that looking foolish is harmful to your health.

You just might discover that looking foolish is far less dangerous than spending your life trying to avoid it.

And you’ll have a lot more fun in the process.
